Nutrition Assessment & Education

Nutrition assessment — anthropometry, clinical signs, dietary history; nutrition education for patients.

🎯 After this chapter you can

  • List methods of nutrition assessment
  • Describe anthropometric measurements
  • Explain how to give nutrition education

In simple words

Nutrition assessment finds out whether a person is well nourished, under-nourished or over-nourished. It uses anthropometry, clinical signs, dietary history and laboratory tests.

Nutrition education teaches patients and families how to choose and prepare healthy food within their means.

Methods of nutrition assessment

Method What it is Examples
Anthropometry Body measurements Weight, height, mid-upper arm circumference
Clinical Signs of deficiency Pallor, bleeding gums, bitot spots
Dietary What the person eats 24-hour recall, food frequency
Laboratory Blood tests Haemoglobin, serum albumin

Anthropometric measurements

  • Weight — compared with height for age.
  • Height — compared with age.
  • Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) — quick screen for acute malnutrition in children.
  • Body Mass Index (BMI) — weight (kg) ÷ height (m)².

Nutrition education

  • Use simple language and local examples.
  • Show, don’t just tell — use food models or pictures.
  • Involve the family.
  • Give one or two key messages at a time.

🔴 MUAC screens child malnutrition

Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a quick screen for acute malnutrition in children. Below the cutoff, the child needs urgent nutritional care.

Where the nurse uses this

  • Admission screening — weigh and measure every patient; note deficiency signs.
  • Children — measure MUAC; plot weight on growth charts.
  • Nutrition education — teach balanced diet, hygiene and therapeutic diets simply.
  • Refer — refer malnourished patients to the dietitian or doctor.
  • Follow-up — re-assess to see if nutrition is improving.

🔴 Most important for exams

  1. Nutrition assessment uses anthropometry, clinical signs, dietary history and laboratory tests.
  2. Anthropometry: weight, height, MUAC, BMI.
  3. MUAC quickly screens acute malnutrition in children.
  4. BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)².
  5. Nutrition education uses simple language, local examples and family involvement.

⭐ Important for exams

  1. Clinical signs: pallor (anaemia), bleeding gums (vitamin C), bitot spots (vitamin A).
  2. Dietary history: 24-hour recall or food frequency questionnaire.
  3. Laboratory: haemoglobin and serum albumin.
  4. Give one or two key nutrition messages at a time.

📌 Memory trick

Assessment methods: “A-C-D-L” — Anthropometry, Clinical, Dietary, Laboratory.

60-second revision

  • Nutrition assessment = anthropometry, clinical, dietary, laboratory.
  • Measurements: weight, height, MUAC, BMI.
  • MUAC screens child malnutrition.
  • Deficiency signs: pallor, bleeding gums, bitot spots.
  • Education: simple, local, family, few messages at a time.

Test yourself

MUAC is used to screen:

Answer: B. MUAC (mid-upper arm circumference) quickly screens acute malnutrition in children.

BMI is calculated as:

Answer: B. BMI = weight in kilograms divided by height in metres squared.

Bitot spots indicate deficiency of:

Answer: B. Bitot spots on the eye indicate vitamin A deficiency.

A 24-hour recall is a:

Answer: B. A 24-hour recall asks what the person ate in the past 24 hours.

Nutrition education is best given:

Answer: B. Use simple language and local examples, and involve the family.
